questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Why people smile more when they are nervous or worried
How many muscles we have in our face and how they work
Computers that can tell real smiles from fake ones
How to take better photos of people who don't like smiling
questions.why: Neil says it's about how computers may tell real smiles from fake smiles better than humans.

questions.q: Why does Sam question Neil's greeting at the start?
options: She finds it hard to tell if a smile is real
Neil forgot her name when he said hello
Neil wasn't smiling and looked very bored
She was in a bad mood after a long journey
questions.why: She says she finds it difficult to tell if someone is really smiling or faking it.

options: A psychologist who studies happiness
A film director
A presenter on BBC Inside Science
A professor of visual computing
questions.why: Neil introduces him as a professor of visual computing at the University of Bradford.

questions.q: How does the software identify emotions?
options: By listening to the person's voice
By studying facial muscle movements on video
By measuring heart rate
By asking people how they feel
questions.why: He explains it looks at facial muscle movement through video frames.

questions.q: What is special about how the software works?
options: It works only on photographs
It needs several days to analyse data
It works instantly, while the person is talking
It only works in a laboratory
questions.why: Sam explains it works in real time, with no delay.

questions.q: How did the researchers get examples of real smiles?
options: By showing people funny films
By telling people jokes
By using photos from social media
By paying people to smile
questions.why: They sat people on a chair and showed some funny movies.

questions.q: How did they collect fake smiles?
options: They used actors from films
They drew them on a computer
They showed sad films
They asked people to pretend to smile
questions.why: Professor Ugail says, 'we ask them to pretend to smile.'

options: It is about as good as humans
It is right about 90% of the time
It is right about half the time
It is always right
questions.why: Neil says it gets it right 90% of the time, much higher than humans.
